newsitem.title: SOUTH KOREA: S.Korean students riot during massacre anniversary.
newsitem.headline: S.Korean students riot during massacre anniversary.

text.p: Radical students hurling rocks and firebombs battled riot police on Saturday in the South Korean city of Kwangju as residents mourned victims of a 1980 army massacre.
Violence erupted on the eve of the anniversary of the Kwangju killings, which this year is being commemorated by the government for the first time.
The massacre has left deep scars on the nation, but a healing is now under way following the jailing of the two main perpetrators of the slaughter -- former presidents Chun Doo Hwan and Roh Tae-woo.
More than 200 people died, by official count, when paratroopers stormed the southwestern city to crush an armed revolt against martial law imposed by then-general Chun.
Most of the dead were students.

On Saturday, some 2,500 students tried to march out of Chosun University to join a concert in a plaza outside the provincial government building, scene of the worst carnage during the military onslaught.
They rained petrol bombs on ranks of riot police blocking their way, who responded with barrages of tear gas.
Inside the campus, funeral rites were conducted around the coffin of a student who died of a heart attack during anti-government protests in March.

Pitched battles briefly died down after a stray tear gas canister ignited a blaze in a pool hall, which was eventually extinguished by fire officers. Several police officers were carried away hurt during the fighting.
Giant speakers blared traditional Korean music across the plaza, filled with thousands of citizens, many of them in family groups with children.
On a large stage, a dance group in black and white martial arts outfits re-enacted scenes of the massacre.
Portraits of some of the victims were hung along the streets together with pictures of soldiers killing old men and women.

Earlier, Kwangju mayor Song Eun-jong had led mourners in a newly dedicated cemetery to victims of the massacre. It was the first time South Korean officials had presided over anniversary events to mark the bloodletting.
Chun was sentenced to life in prison and Roh to 17 years on charges of mutiny, sedition and corruption. Their final appeals were dismissed in April.

Wailing and sobbing, about 200 relatives of the victims gathered in front of a fruit-laden altar at the "May 18 Cemetery" on hills outside Kwangju where bodies of 124 victims have been laid in fresh graves.
The remains were moved this month from their original resting place adjacent to the new cemetery.
Elderly women relatives dressed in traditional white mourning robes cried out the names of sons and daughters who perished.
Residents say several thousand may have been killed by machinegun fire and bayonets and their bodies buried in unmarked graves or burned.

The focal point of the new cemetery is a 40-metre-high (131 foot) memorial in the form of stylised hands clasping an egg, a symbol of life. Two statues flanking the memorial depict students brandishing rifles in heroic style.
Graves with simple granite headstones are laid out in neat rows on a lawn.

A total of 137 bodies of massacre victims lay in the old cemetery. Some relatives have refused to move the remains until the new cemetery is designated a "National Cemetery", whose occupants are honoured as heroes.
"They've been neglected for too long and now they are finally being honoured," said Park Kong-soon, president of the Kwangju Bereaved Families' Association.
